seo_title: Grade 5 Equivalent Fractions and Mixed Numbers Worksheets (Ontario Math): Free with Answer Key
standard_text: Use drawings and models to represent, compare, and order fractions representing the individual portions that result from multiple wholes being shared by any number of sharers, and equivalent fractions from halves to twelfths, including improper fractions and mixed numbers

key_big: Equivalent fractions: multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the same number.
key_sub: 3/4 = 9/12 (× 3) and 8/12 = 2/3 (÷ 4). 11/4 = 2 3/4, because there are two 4s in 11 with 3 left over. A bigger denominator means smaller parts: 1/8 < 1/4.
body_html:
Equivalent fractions

Equivalent fractions show the same amount. To find one, multiply (or divide) the numerator and the denominator by the same number. The parts get smaller, but there are more of them.

Example

34 = ?12

4 × 3 = 12, so multiply the numerator by 3 too: 3 × 3 = 9.

Answer: 912

Simplest form

A fraction is in simplest form when no number except 1 divides both the numerator and the denominator. Divide both by the greatest number you can.

Example

Write 812 in simplest form.

4 divides both 8 and 12. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3.

Answer: 23

Sharing wholes

When some wholes are shared equally, each person gets wholes ÷ people. 3 pancakes shared by 4 friends: each friend gets 34 of a pancake.

Improper fractions and mixed numbers

An improper fraction such as 114 is greater than 1. A mixed number such as 2 34 shows the same amount as wholes and a fraction.

Example

Write 175 as a mixed number.

There are three 5s in 17 (15), with 2 left over.

Answer: 3 25

Example

Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.

2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13.

Answer: 135

Comparing and ordering

Give the fractions the same denominator, then compare the numerators. If the numerators are the same, the fraction with the smaller denominator is greater, because its parts are bigger.

Example

Order 34, 58 and 12 from least to greatest.

Use eighths: 34 = 68, 58, 12 = 48.

Answer: 12, 58, 34

Example

Which is greater: 74 or 1 12?

74 = 1 34. Both have 1 whole, and 34 > 24.

Answer: 74

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the same number to the top and bottom: 23 = 45Multiply or divide, never add: 23 = 46
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: 18 > 14A bigger denominator means smaller parts: 18 < 14
Multiplying only the numerator: 23 = 43Multiply both: 23 = 46
2 35 = 65Wholes × denominator, then add the numerator: 2 × 5 + 3 = 13, so 135

faq.q: What do Grade 5 students learn about fractions in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Ontario Grade 5 math curriculum, students use drawings and models to find equivalent fractions from halves to twelfths, work with improper fractions and mixed numbers, and compare and order fractions. They also model sharing several wholes equally, such as 3 pancakes shared by 4 friends.

faq.q: How do you find an equivalent fraction?
faq.a: Multiply or divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number. For example, 3/4 = 9/12 (both × 3) and 8/12 = 2/3 (both ÷ 4). Adding the same number to both does not work.

faq.q: How do you change an improper fraction to a mixed number?
faq.a: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The answer is the number of wholes and the remainder is the new numerator, so 17/5 = 3 2/5. To go back, multiply the wholes by the denominator and add the numerator: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

faq.q: How do you compare fractions with different denominators?
faq.a: Change them so both have the same denominator, then compare the numerators. For 2/3 and 7/12, 2/3 = 8/12, so 2/3 is greater. A bigger denominator alone does not mean a bigger fraction: 1/8 is less than 1/4.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 34 is shaded. How many eighths are equal to 34?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each fourth is the same as 2 eighths, so 3 fourths line up with 3 × 2 = 6 eighths. So 34 = 68.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 23 is shaded. How many twelfths are equal to 23?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each third is the same as 4 twelfths, so 2 thirds line up with 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths. So 23 = 812.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 45 is shaded. How many tenths are equal to 45?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each fifth is the same as 2 tenths, so 4 fifths line up with 4 × 2 = 8 tenths. So 45 = 810.

items.q: Use the fraction wall. 12 is shaded. How many twelfths are equal to 12?
items.e: Look down the fraction wall. Each half is the same as 6 twelfths, so 1 half lines up with 1 × 6 = 6 twelfths. So 12 = 612.

items.q: 912 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 3. Which equivalent fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 4 groups and 3 of them are shaded, so 912 = 34. This is the same as dividing 9 and 12 by 3.

items.q: 410 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 2. Which equivalent fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 5 groups and 2 of them are shaded, so 410 = 25. This is the same as dividing 4 and 10 by 2.

items.q: 68 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 2. Which equivalent fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 4 groups and 3 of them are shaded, so 68 = 34. This is the same as dividing 6 and 8 by 2.

items.q: 1012 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 2. Which equivalent fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 6 groups and 5 of them are shaded, so 1012 = 56. This is the same as dividing 10 and 12 by 2.

items.q: 69 of the bar is shaded. The thick lines make groups of 3. Which equivalent fraction does the bar show?
items.e: There are 3 groups and 2 of them are shaded, so 69 = 23. This is the same as dividing 6 and 9 by 3.

items.q: 3 pancakes are shared equally by 4 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How much does each friend get?
c: 34 of a pancake
14 of a pancake
43 of a pancake
13 of a pancake
items.e: Cut each of the 3 pancakes into 4 equal parts. Each person gets 1 part from every pancake: 3 × 14 = 34 of a pancake. This is the same as 3 ÷ 4.

items.q: 2 granola bars are shared equally by 3 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How much does each friend get?
c: 32 of a granola bar
23 of a granola bar
12 of a granola bar
13 of a granola bar
items.e: Cut each of the 2 granola bars into 3 equal parts. Each person gets 1 part from every granola bar: 2 × 13 = 23 of a granola bar. This is the same as 2 ÷ 3.

items.q: 4 sub sandwiches are shared equally by 5 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How much does each friend get?
c: 54 of a sub sandwich
15 of a sub sandwich
45 of a sub sandwich
14 of a sub sandwich
items.e: Cut each of the 4 sub sandwiches into 5 equal parts. Each person gets 1 part from every sub sandwich: 4 × 15 = 45 of a sub sandwich. This is the same as 4 ÷ 5.

items.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 12?
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by 6: 1 × 6 = 6 and 2 × 6 = 12. So 12 = 612. Adding 5 to both (67) does not keep the amount the same.

items.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 34?
items.e: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by 3: 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 3 = 12. So 34 = 912. 56 adds 2 to both numbers, 64 multiplies only the top, and 38 multiplies only the bottom.

items.q: 25 = ?10
items.e: Look at the denominators: 5 × 2 = 10. Multiply the numerator by 2 too: 2 × 2 = 4. So 25 = 410.

items.q: 34 = ?12
items.e: Look at the denominators: 4 × 3 = 12. Multiply the numerator by 3 too: 3 × 3 = 9. So 34 = 912.

items.q: 23 = ?9
items.e: Look at the denominators: 3 × 3 = 9. Multiply the numerator by 3 too: 2 × 3 = 6. So 23 = 69.

items.q: 56 = 10?
items.e: Look at the numerators: 5 × 2 = 10. Multiply the denominator by 2 too: 6 × 2 = 12. So 56 = 1012. Adding 5 to the top and the bottom (1011) does not keep the amount the same.

items.q: 812 = ?3
items.e: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so divide the numerator by 4 too: 8 ÷ 4 = 2. So 812 = 23.

items.q: 1012 = 5?
items.e: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, so divide the denominator by 2 too: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. So 1012 = 56. Taking 5 from both (to get 57) changes the amount.

items.q: Which fraction is in simplest form?
items.e: 58 is in simplest form, because no number except 1 divides both 5 and 8. The others can be divided: 46 = 23, 610 = 35, 39 = 13.

items.q: Which fraction is in simplest form?
items.e: 712 is in simplest form: 7 and 12 have no common factor except 1. 912 = 34, 210 = 15 and 48 = 12 can all be simplified.

items.q: Write 68 in simplest form.
items.e: 2 is the greatest number that divides both 6 and 8. 6 ÷ 2 = 3 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. So 68 = 34.

items.q: Write 410 in simplest form.
items.e: 2 is the greatest number that divides both 4 and 10. 4 ÷ 2 = 2 and 10 ÷ 2 = 5. So 410 = 25.

items.q: Write 39 in simplest form.
items.e: 3 is the greatest number that divides both 3 and 9. 3 ÷ 3 = 1 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3. So 39 = 13.

items.q: Write 810 in simplest form.
items.e: 2 is the greatest number that divides both 8 and 10. 8 ÷ 2 = 4 and 10 ÷ 2 = 5. So 810 = 45.

items.q: Write 69 in simplest form.
items.e: 3 is the greatest number that divides both 6 and 9. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3. So 69 = 23.

items.q: Write 412 in simplest form.
items.e: 4 is the greatest number that divides both 4 and 12. 4 ÷ 4 = 1 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. So 412 = 13. (Dividing by 2 gives 26, which can still be simplified.)

items.q: Write 28 in simplest form.
items.e: 2 is the greatest number that divides both 2 and 8. 2 ÷ 2 = 1 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. So 28 = 14.

items.q: Write 912 in simplest form.
items.e: 3 is the greatest number that divides both 9 and 12. 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4. So 912 = 34.

items.q: Write 1012 in simplest form.
items.e: 2 is the greatest number that divides both 10 and 12. 10 ÷ 2 = 5 and 12 ÷ 2 = 6. So 1012 = 56.

items.q: Write 812 in simplest form.
items.e: 4 is the greatest number that divides both 8 and 12. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 12 ÷ 4 = 3. So 812 = 23. (Dividing by 2 gives 46, which can still be simplified.)

items.q: Which fraction is not equivalent to 23?
items.e: 45 is not equivalent to 23: 2 was added to the numerator and the denominator, and adding changes the amount. The others are equivalent, because both numbers were multiplied by the same number.

items.q: Which fraction is not equivalent to 12?
items.e: 34 is not equivalent to 12: 2 was added to the numerator and the denominator, and adding changes the amount. The others are equivalent, because both numbers were multiplied by the same number.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 114 are shaded. Write this as a mixed number.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 3 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 114 = 2 34.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 83 are shaded. Write this as a mixed number.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 2 bars are full and 2 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 83 = 2 23.

items.q: Each bar is 1 whole. 75 are shaded. Write this as a mixed number.
items.e: Each bar is 1 whole. 1 bar is full and 2 more parts are shaded in the last bar. So 75 = 1 25.

items.q: 5 pancakes are shared equally by 4 friends. The shaded parts are one friend’s share. How many pancakes does each friend get?
c: 14 of a pancake
45 of a pancake
items.e: Each friend gets 14 of each of the 5 pancakes: 5 × 14 = 54. 4 fourths make 1 whole, with 1 fourth left over. So each friend gets 1 14 pancakes.

items.q: Which letter shows 74?
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. 74 = 1 34: go to 1, then 3 more marks. That is letter B.

items.q: Which letter shows 136?
items.e: Each whole is split into 6 equal parts, so each mark is 16. 136 = 2 16: go to 2, then 1 more mark. That is letter D.

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 3 equal parts, so each mark is 13. The arrow is 2 marks after 2. So it shows 2 23 (= 83).

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 2 equal parts, so each mark is 12. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 12 (= 52).

items.q: What number does the arrow show? Give a mixed number.
items.e: Each whole is split into 4 equal parts, so each mark is 14. The arrow is 1 mark after 2. So it shows 2 14 (= 94).

items.q: Write 135 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 5s are in 13? 2 × 5 = 10, so there are 2 wholes. 13 − 10 = 3 fifths left over. So 135 = 2 35.

items.q: Write 174 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 4s are in 17? 4 × 4 = 16, so there are 4 wholes. 17 − 16 = 1 fourth left over. So 174 = 4 14.

items.q: Write 196 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 6s are in 19? 3 × 6 = 18, so there are 3 wholes. 19 − 18 = 1 sixth left over. So 196 = 3 16.

items.q: Write 2310 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 10s are in 23? 2 × 10 = 20, so there are 2 wholes. 23 − 20 = 3 tenths left over. So 2310 = 2 310.

items.q: Write 298 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 8s are in 29? 3 × 8 = 24, so there are 3 wholes. 29 − 24 = 5 eighths left over. So 298 = 3 58.

items.q: Write 2512 as a mixed number.
items.e: How many 12s are in 25? 2 × 12 = 24, so there are 2 wholes. 25 − 24 = 1 twelfth left over. So 2512 = 2 112.

items.q: Write 2 35 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 55, so 2 wholes are 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add the 3: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: Write 3 14 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 44, so 3 wholes are 3 × 4 = 12 fourths. Add the 1: 12 + 1 = 13. So 3 14 = 134.

items.q: Write 4 23 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 33, so 4 wholes are 4 × 3 = 12 thirds. Add the 2: 12 + 2 = 14. So 4 23 = 143.

items.q: Write 1 710 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 1010, so 1 whole is 1 × 10 = 10 tenths. Add the 7: 10 + 7 = 17. So 1 710 = 1710.

items.q: Write 5 38 as an improper fraction.
items.e: Each whole is 88, so 5 wholes are 5 × 8 = 40 eighths. Add the 3: 40 + 3 = 43. So 5 38 = 438.

items.q: Which is greater: 18 or 14?
items.e: The numerators are the same, so compare the size of the parts. Eighths are smaller than fourths, because the whole is cut into more parts. So 14 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 35 or 310?
items.e: The numerators are the same, so compare the size of the parts. Tenths are smaller than fifths, because the whole is cut into more parts. So 35 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 23 or 29?
items.e: The numerators are the same, so compare the size of the parts. Ninths are smaller than thirds, because the whole is cut into more parts. So 23 is greater.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 23 or 712?
items.e: Use twelfths for both: 23 = 812 and 712. 8 > 7, so 23 is greater.

items.q: The bars are the same size. Which is greater: 58 or 34?
items.e: Use eighths for both: 58 and 34 = 68. 6 > 5, so 34 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 35 or 710?
items.e: Use tenths for both: 35 = 610 and 710. 7 > 6, so 710 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 56 or 1112?
items.e: Use twelfths for both: 56 = 1012 and 1112. 11 > 10, so 1112 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 34 or 68?
items.e: Use eighths for both: 34 = 68 and 68. The numerators are the same, so they are equal.

items.q: Which is greater: 12 or 512?
items.e: Use twelfths for both: 12 = 612 and 512. 6 > 5, so 12 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 23 or 34?
items.e: Use twelfths for both: 23 = 812 and 34 = 912. 9 > 8, so 34 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 74 or 1 12?
items.e: 74 = 1 34. Both have 1 whole. Compare the parts: 12 = 24, and 34 > 24. So 74 is greater.

items.q: Which is greater: 2 13 or 83?
items.e: 2 13 = 2 × 3 + 1 = 73. 83 > 73, so 83 is greater. (83 = 2 23.)

items.q: Which is greater: 115 or 2 15?
items.e: 115: 5 × 2 = 10, with 1 fifth left over, so 115 = 2 15. They are equal.

items.q: Which fraction is the greatest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 8: 34 = 68, 58, 12 = 48, 38. The greatest is 68, so the answer is 34.

items.q: Which fraction is the smallest?
items.e: Write them all with the denominator 12: 23 = 812, 56 = 1012, 712, 512. The smallest is 512, so the answer is 512.

34, 58, 12

34, 58, 12
12, 58, 34
58, 34, 12
items.e: Use the denominator 8: 34 = 68, 58, 12 = 48. So the order is 12, 58, 34.

items.q:

23, 712, 56
c: 712, 23, 56
712, 56, 23
56, 23, 712
23, 56, 712
items.e: Use the denominator 12: 23 = 812, 712, 56 = 1012. So the order is 712, 23, 56.

items.q:
Order from greatest to least:
310, 12, 25
c: 310, 12, 25
12, 25, 310
12, 310, 25
310, 25, 12
items.e: Use the denominator 10: 310, 12 = 510, 25 = 410. So the order is 12, 25, 310.

items.q:
Order from least to greatest:
94, 1 12, 2 13
c: 1 12, 2 13, 94
2 13, 94, 1 12
1 12, 94, 2 13
2 13, 1 12, 94
items.e: 94 = 2 14. 1 12 has only 1 whole, so it is the least. Compare 2 14 and 2 13 in twelfths: 14 = 312 and 13 = 412. So the order is 1 12, 94, 2 13.

items.q: Which fraction is between 12 and 34?
items.e: In eighths: 12 = 48 and 34 = 68. 58 is between them. 38 is less than 12. 78 and 56 are more than 34.

items.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Liam eats 34 of it. How many slices does he eat?
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8, so 34 = 68. Liam eats 6 slices.

items.q: A tray of 12 butter tarts is on the table. Maya’s family eats 9 of them. What fraction of the tray is eaten, in simplest form?
items.e: 9 out of 12 = 912. Divide both numbers by 3: 912 = 34.

items.q: Mrs. Patel brings 3 loaves of banana bread for 4 tables. Each table gets an equal share. How much banana bread does each table get?
c: 13 of a loaf
43 of a loaf
34 of a loaf
14 of a loaf
items.e: Cut each loaf into 4 equal parts. Each table gets 1 part of each loaf: 3 × 14 = 34 of a loaf. This is the same as 3 ÷ 4.

items.q: 5 friends share 7 sub sandwiches equally at a soccer tournament. How much does each friend get?
c: 57 of a sandwich
items.e: Each friend gets 15 of each sandwich: 7 × 15 = 75. 5 fifths make 1 whole, with 2 fifths left over. So each friend gets 1 25 sandwiches.

items.q: Group A: 2 pizzas are shared equally by 3 students. Group B: 3 pizzas are shared equally by 4 students. In which group does each student get more pizza?
items.e: Group A: each student gets 23. Group B: each student gets 34. In twelfths: 23 = 812 and 34 = 912. So each student in Group B gets more.

items.q: Olivia’s maple syrup jug holds 35 L. Noah’s jug holds 710 L. Whose jug holds more?
items.e: Use tenths: 35 = 610. 7 tenths is more than 6 tenths, so Noah’s jug holds more.

items.q: Aiden says, “18 is greater than 14, because 8 is greater than 4.” Is he right?
c: Yes. Eighths are bigger than fourths
No. 18 is less than 14
items.e: A bigger denominator means the whole is cut into more, smaller parts. 14 = 28, which is more than 18. So 18 is less than 14.

items.q: Zoe changed 23 into an equivalent fraction and wrote 45. What did she do wrong?
c: She added 2 to the top and the bottom
She multiplied only the numerator by 2
items.e: 2 + 2 = 4 and 3 + 2 = 5. Adding changes the amount. Multiply both numbers by 2 instead: 23 = 46.

items.q: Ethan runs 74 km in the Terry Fox Run. Write this distance as a mixed number.
items.e: 4 fourths make 1 km. 7 − 4 = 3 fourths are left over. So 74 km = 1 34 km.

items.q: Each glass holds 14 L of milk. Chloe fills 9 glasses. How much milk is that, as a mixed number?
items.e: 9 glasses of 14 L = 94 L. 4 fourths make 1 L, so 8 fourths make 2 L, with 1 fourth left over: 2 14 L.

items.q: Arjun says 2 35 = 65. What is the correct improper fraction?
items.e: Arjun multiplied 2 × 3. Instead, 2 wholes = 2 × 5 = 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths: 10 + 3 = 13. So 2 35 = 135.

items.q: Four students measure their ribbons. Mateo: 34 m. Hana: 78 m. Kai: 58 m. Sofia: 12 m. Who has the longest ribbon?
items.e: Use eighths: 34 = 68, 78, 58, 12 = 48. The longest is Hana’s ribbon.

items.q: Priya’s family paddles 2 12 km on a canoe trip. How many half kilometres is that?
items.e: 2 km = 2 × 2 = 4 halves. Add 1 more half: 4 + 1 = 5 halves. So 2 12 km = 52 km.

items.q: Students eat 19 slices of pizza on a field trip. Each pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. How many pizzas do they eat?
items.e: 6 slices make 1 pizza. 3 × 6 = 18, and 19 − 18 = 1 slice is left. So 196 = 3 16 pizzas.

items.q: Three classes each have the same size pot of paint for a mural. Grade 5A uses 56 of its pot, Grade 5B uses 712 and Grade 5C uses 23. Which class uses the least paint?
items.e: Use twelfths: 56 = 1012, 712, 23 = 812. The smallest is 712, so Grade 5B uses the least. 12 is the biggest denominator, but that does not make it the biggest fraction.

items.q: Emma gets 710 on a spelling quiz. Owen gets 45 on the same quiz. Who did better?
items.e: Use tenths: 45 = 810. 8 is more than 7, so Owen did better.

items.q: Nathan practises hockey for 1 12 hours. Benjamin practises for 54 hours. Who practises longer?
items.e: 54 = 1 14. Both have 1 whole hour. Compare the parts: 12 = 24, which is more than 14. So Nathan practises longer.

items.q: 4 friends at the cottage share 6 granola bars equally. How many granola bars does each friend get?
c: 46 of a bar
items.e: Each friend gets 6 ÷ 4 = 64 bars. 4 fourths make 1 whole, with 2 fourths left over: 1 24 = 1 12 bars.

items.q: A maple cookie recipe needs 2 14 cups of flour. Leah only has a 14 cup scoop. How many scoops does she need?
items.e: 1 cup = 4 fourths, so 2 cups = 8 fourths. Add 1 more fourth: 8 + 1 = 9 scoops. So 2 14 = 94.

items.q: Jayden has a board 94 m long. He says it is longer than 2 m. Is he right?
c: No. 94 m = 1 14 m
Yes. 94 m = 2 14 m
No. 94 m = 49 m
items.e: 4 fourths make 1 m, so 8 fourths make 2 m. 9 − 8 = 1 fourth is left over. So 94 m = 2 14 m, which is longer than 2 m.
